Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: What is standard practice for cleaning woven-wire metal test sieves between different metal-alloy powders so that one alloy does not cross-contaminate the next? Our specific case: we just sieved a bronze (Cu-Sn) powder through a 63 um (about 230 mesh) and a 250 um (about 60 mesh) test sieve, and next we want to sieve an aluminum-alloy powder (e.g., AlSi10Mg or a new Al alloy) through the same two sieves as feedstock for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Please cover, with citations, DOIs or standard numbers:

(1) Cleaning methods for test sieves (ASTM E11 / ISO 3310-1) per standards and sieve-maker guidance (e.g., ASTM B214, ASTM E2427, ISO 2591-1, MPIF Standard 05, and sieve-maker handbooks), and how they differ between a fine 63 um mesh and a coarser 250 um mesh: dry methods (tapping, soft brushing from the underside, vacuum, low-pressure air) versus wet methods (ultrasonic bath: frequency, detergent or solvent, time, temperature), rinsing and drying (temperature limits for epoxy- or solder-bonded mesh), and what damages fine meshes (stiff or wire brushes, pushing trapped particles through with needles, high-pressure air, overloading).

(2) Whether cleaning alone is considered enough for additive-manufacturing-grade powder, or whether dedicated sieves for each alloy family are standard practice (e.g., ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52904, NASA MSFC-SPEC-3717, or industry powder-handling guidance). How do labs verify that a sieve is clean before switching alloys (backlit or stereo-microscope inspection of the mesh, weighing, wipe or tape tests, running a sacrificial flush portion of the new powder, SEM-EDS or ICP-OES of the first aluminum powder for Cu and Sn)?

(3) How much Cu-Sn particle contamination matters in aluminum LPBF powder: documented cross-contamination cases in powder bed fusion (foreign-alloy particles in Ti-6Al-4V, aluminum, nickel or steel powders), the defects they cause (inclusions, unmelted particles, Cu-rich regions, cracking, corrosion), and any quantified tolerance limits or detection thresholds.

(4) Safety: any hazard from residual bronze (possibly surface-oxidized, CuO/Cu2O) mixing with fine aluminum powder (thermite, combustible dust, NFPA 484), and how to safely clean aluminum-powder residue off the sieves afterwards (wet or ultrasonic cleaning producing hydrogen, wet aluminum fines, solvent choice, waste disposal).

(5) A step-by-step cleaning and verification procedure suitable for a small university lab, distinguishing recommendations that are well supported by the literature or standards from those that rest on vendor guidance or common practice.

Context: university materials lab making small batches of alloy powder (ultrasonic atomization) for LPBF, sieving by hand or on a sieve shaker with standard round test sieves.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing is now taking the lead over traditional manufacturing techniques in applications such as aerospace and biomedicine, which are characterized by low production volumes and high levels of customization. While fulfilling these requirements is the strength of metal additive manufacturing, respecting the tight tolerances typical of the mentioned applications is a harder task to accomplish. Powder bed fusion (PBF) is a class of additive manufacturing in which layers of metal powder are fused on top of each other by a high-energy beam (laser or electron beam) according to a computer-aided design (CAD) model. The quality of raw powders for PBF affects the mechanical properties of additively manufactured parts strongly, and therefore it is crucial to avoid the presence of any source of contamination, particularly cross-contamination. In this study, the identification and quantification of cross-contamination in powders of Ti-6Al-4V and maraging steel was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) techniques. Experimental results showed an overall good reliability of the developed method, opening the way for applications in machine learning environments.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and direct laser deposition (DLD) are the two main processes currently used in the additive manufacturing (AM) of metals. For both methods, metal powders are used as feedstock, and they must present specific physical and chemical properties to ensure optimal processing and reliable and reproducible printing results. Particle morphology, size distribution, and flowability, among other factors, depend on the powder production process and directly influence the processing parameters and physical characteristics of the parts built by AM. This systematic review presents different concepts involving L-PBF and DLD manufacturing and the application of metal powders. The methods used to produce and characterize metal powders and the modification techniques to improve their processability by AM are detailed and discussed. Environmental and health risks are also presented, and safety measures that must be considered while handling metal powders. Some key topics requiring attention for further development are highlighted. Graphical abstract

Abstract:
The processing of pure copper (Cu) has been a challenge for laser-based additive manufacturing for many years since copper powders have a high reflectivity of up to 83% of electromagnetic radiation at a wavelength of 1070 nm. In this study, Cu particles were coated with sub-micrometer tungsten (W) particles to increase the laser beam absorptivity. The coated powders were processed by powder bed fusion-laser beam for metals (PBF-LB/M) with a conventional laser system of <300 watts laser power and a wavelength of 1070 nm. Two different powder manufacturing routes were developed. The first manufacturing route was gas atomization combined with a milling process by a planetary mill. The second manufacturing method was gas atomization with particle co-injection, where a separate W particle jet was sprayed into the atomized Cu jet. As part of the investigations, an extensive characterization of powder and additively manufactured test specimens was carried out. The specimens of Cu/W powders manufactured by the milling process have shown superior results. The laser absorptivity of the Cu/W powder was increased from 22.5% (pure Cu powder) to up to 71.6% for powders with 3 vol% W. In addition, a relative density of test specimens up to 98.2% (optically) and 95.6% (Archimedes) was reached. Furthermore, thermal conductivity was measured by laser flash analysis (LFA) and thermo-optical measurement (TOM). By using eddy current measurement, the electrical conductivity was analyzed. In comparison to the Cu reference, a thermal conductivity of 88.9% and an electrical conductivity of 85.8% were determined. Moreover, the Vickers hardness was measured. The effect of porosity on conductivity properties and hardness was investigated and showed a linear correlation. Finally, a demonstrator was built in which a wall thickness of down to 200 µm was achieved. This demonstrates that the Cu/W composite can be used for heat exchangers, heat sinks, and coils.

The excerpt provides limited, general cleaning and maintenance guidance for woven-wire metal powder test sieves. It identifies ISO 3310/1 and ASTM E11 among the standards specifying sieve series, and identifies ISO 4497, ASTM B214, and MPIF Standard 05 as standards associated with carrying out sieve analysis. For cleaning, it states that brushing may be attempted first when particles are entrapped in sieve openings; if brushing does not remove them, an ultrasonic wash with a wetting agent is required. The excerpt does not specify a dry-brushing direction or underside technique, nor does it give different instructions for 63- versus 250-micrometer sieves. It also contains no verified ultrasonic frequency, bath duration, temperature, detergent identity, solvent, rinse procedure, or drying conditions. For sieve condition, it warns that damaged sieves may have stretched, distorted, or torn mesh, recommends regular microscopic examination, and notes that epoxy has been used to repair small damage. However, it gives no epoxy formulation, solder-bond procedure, curing or bonding temperature, or acceptance criteria. Thus, the passage supports only the broad cleaning sequence and cited standards; the detailed parameters in the question are not documented in this excerpt.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Metal additive manufacturing (AM) in AlSi10Mg is enabling a new generation of lightweight and functionally optimised mirrors for aerospace, astronomy, and Earth observation. Common manufacturing routes use single point diamond turning to generate the reflective surface in the AlSi10Mg alloy leading to good reflectivity in the near infrared and visible wavelengths, further, it is often a precursor to optical polishing for shorter wavelength applications. However, the good reflectivity can be detrimentally affected by the generation of scratches on the reflective surface and this in turn limits the uptake in AM to create lightweight mirrors. Therefore, understanding the initiation of the scratch and its origin, supports improving AM mirror fabrication chains and harnessing the design benefit of AM. This study collated six AM AlSi10Mg mirrors from different projects, built using four different printers in three different production environments, and analysed the scratch initiation sites for morphology and elemental composition using scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy. The results highlighted scratches generated by aluminium oxide (Al
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ), a contaminant almost inherent in the AM process; titanium alloy (Ti6Al4V), a contaminant from printer powder exchanges; and Ti6Al4V and stainless-steel alloy (316L), contaminants from the manufacturing production environment. The results imply that to reduce scratches, AlSi10Mg only printers should be used with minimum powder recycling, further, printers should operate robust cleanliness within the manufacturing production environment to avoid cross contamination between printers.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder bed fusion (PBF) and directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing use feedstock powders that contain metals associated with skin diseases. We performed a survey of surface contamination and limited task-based dermal exposure assessment (four employees) at a PBF and DED facility. Skin wipes of wrists for two employees in the PBF room had higher post-task levels of chromium, cobalt, molybdenum, and nickel. Personal clothing worn by PBF employees showed evidence of contamination with metals as did personal protective equipment (PPE). Microscopy analysis documented contamination of metals throughout most areas of the facility. Levels of metals on surfaces throughout the facility were (ng/cm2) <5.0–7247 (aluminum), <0.2–4899 (chromium), <background-6.0 (chromium VI), 0.03–468.1 (cobalt), 1.6–100.0 (copper), 32.9–19,000 (iron), 0.01–789.0 (molybdenum), 0.1–12,058 (nickel), 0.1–482.8 (titanium), and 0.07–9.3 (vanadium). Levels were significantly lower in administrative areas compared with the production area but generally did not differ among powder handling and non-powder handling rooms in production. The small number of participants in the dermal exposure assessment and uniqueness of the facility might limit generalizability of the results. At least for this facility, steps to lower skin contact with metals can include washing, consistent use of PPE, and increasing awareness of dermal hazards among workers. Approaches to reduce migration of metals throughout a facility can include using adhesive (“tacky”) mats and boot covers and frequent wet cleaning of floors, tools, handles, and high touch surfaces.</jats:p>

Abstract:
BACKGROUND
Amidst the rapidly emerging additive manufacturing (AM) industry, not enough attention has been given to dermal exposure, with only one previous study that assessed dermal exposure to metals. Our study aimed to characterise a cobalt (Co)-chrome (Cr) alloy feedstock powder (CO-538) in terms of particle size, shape, and elemental composition, and assess dermal exposure and workplace surface contamination during powder bed fusion AM.


METHODS
Particle size distribution (PSD) and shape of the virgin and used feedstock powder were determined using static image and scanning electron microscopy analyses. The elemental composition of powders was established using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry. A removal wipe sampling method using Ghostwipes was performed on AM operators' skin at various locations (index finger, palm, wrist, back of the hand, and neck), before and after each AM processing phase. Workplace surfaces (both AM and non-AM areas) were also sampled before and after each shift using a removal wipe method to measure surface contamination.


RESULTS
PSD analysis revealed a significant difference (P ≤ 0.05) in median size, with used powder exhibiting smaller particles than virgin, where 10% of particles were smaller than the given diameter. Additionally, significant differences (P ≤ 0.05) were noted in the mean circularity and convexity between virgin and used powders, indicating that used powder particles were more irregular and rougher compared to virgin. The CO-538 feedstock powder contained Co, Cr, molybdenum (Mo), aluminium (Al), iron (Fe), and Ni. These metals were also detected on the skin of AM operators and on surfaces within the AM and non-AM areas of the facility. Dermal exposure occurred on all of the anatomical areas, with the highest total metal concentration detected on the index finger during the post-processing phase of AM. The highest full-shift geometric mean GM concentration of each metal was detected on the finger and followed a trend of Co > Cr > Fe > Al > Mo > Ni. Surface contamination occurred on all AM and non-AM sampling areas after a full shift.


CONCLUSIONS
Dermal exposure to all CO-538 alloy metal constituents occurred on all sampled anatomical areas during all three processing phases. Measurable concentrations of metals that were detected on all sampled surfaces indicate that cross-contamination between AM and non-AM areas occurs and that these surfaces may act as a secondary source of exposure. There is thus a need for control measures to be implemented in AM facilities to eliminate or reduce surface metal contamination and dermal exposure.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is dynamically developing and finding applications in different industries. The quality of input material is a part of the process and of the final product quality. That is why understanding the influence of powder reuse on the properties of bulk specimens is crucial for ensuring the repeatable AM process chain. The presented study investigated the possibility of continuous reuse of AlSi7Mg0.6 powder in the laser powder bed fusion process (LPBF). To date, there is no study of AlSi7Mg0.6 powder reuse in the LPBF process to be found in the literature. This study aims to respond to this gap. The five batches of AlSi7Mg0.6 powder and five bulk LPBF samples series were characterised using different techniques. The following characteristics of powders were analysed: the powder size distribution (PSD), the morphology (scanning electron microscopy—SEM), the flowability (rotating drum analysis), and laser light absorption (spectrophotometry). Bulk samples were characterised for microstructure (SEM), chemical composition (X-ray fluorescence spectrometry—XRF), porosity (computed tomography—CT) and mechanical properties (tensile, hardness). The powder was reused in subsequent processes without adding (recycling/rejuvenation) virgin powder (collective ageing powder reuse strategy). All tested powders (powders P0–P4) and bulk samples (series S0–S3) show repeatable properties, with changes observed within error limits. Samples manufactured within the fifth reuse cycle (series S4) showed some mean value changes of measured characteristics indicating initial degradation. However, these changes also mostly fit within error limits. Therefore, the collective ageing powder reuse strategy is considered to give repeatable LPBF process results and is recommended for the AlSi7Mg0.6 alloy within at least five consecutive LPBF processes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Quality is a key determinant in deploying new processes, products, or services and influences the adoption of emerging manufacturing technologies. The advent of additive manufacturing (AM) as a manufacturing process has the potential to revolutionize a host of enterprise-related functions from production to the supply chain. The unprecedented level of design flexibility and expanded functionality offered by AM, coupled with greatly reduced lead times, can potentially pave the way for mass customization. However, widespread application of AM is currently hampered by technical challenges in process repeatability and quality management. The breakthrough effect of six sigma (6S) has been demonstrated in traditional manufacturing industries (e.g., semiconductor and automotive industries) in the context of quality planning, control, and improvement through the intensive use of data, statistics, and optimization. 6S entails a data-driven DMAIC methodology of five steps—define, measure, analyze, improve, and control. Notwithstanding the sustained successes of the 6S knowledge body in a variety of established industries ranging from manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, and beyond, there is a dearth of concentrated application of 6S quality management approaches in the context of AM. In this article, we propose to design, develop, and implement the new DMAIC methodology for the 6S quality management of AM. First, we define the specific quality challenges arising from AM layerwise fabrication and mass customization (even one-of-a-kind production). Second, we present a review of AM metrology and sensing techniques, from materials through design, process, and environment, to postbuild inspection. Third, we contextualize a framework for realizing the full potential of data from AM systems and emphasize the need for analytical methods and tools. We propose and delineate the utility of new data-driven analytical methods, including deep learning, machine learning, and network science, to characterize and model the interrelationships between engineering design, machine setting, process variability, and final build quality. Fourth, we present the methodologies of ontology analytics, design of experiments (DOE), and simulation analysis for AM system improvements. In closing, new process control approaches are discussed to optimize the action plans, once an anomaly is detected, with specific consideration of lead time and energy consumption. We posit that this work will catalyze more in-depth investigations and multidisciplinary research efforts to accelerate the application of 6S quality management in AM.

## 1. Thermal Decomposition Behavior and Thermal Safety of Nitrocellulose with Different Shape CuO and Al/CuO Nanothermites

    title = "Thermal Decomposition Behavior and Thermal Safety of Nitrocellulose with Different Shape CuO and Al/CuO Nanothermites",
    year = "2020",

    volume = "10",

    url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/nano10040725",
    publisher = "MDPI AG",
    issue = "4",
    issn = "2079-4991"
}


Abstract:
Bamboo leaf-like CuO(b) and flaky-shaped CuO(f) were prepared by the hydrothermal method, and then combined with Al nanoparticles to form Al/CuO(b) and Al/CuO(f) by the ultrasonic dispersion method. The phase, composition, morphology, and structure of the composites were characterized by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy scattering spectrometer (EDS). The compatibility of CuO, Al/CuO and nitrocellulose (NC) was evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The effects of CuO and Al/CuO on the thermal decomposition of NC were also studied. The results show that the thermal decomposition reactions of CuO-NC composite, Al/CuO-NC composite, and NC follow the same kinetic mechanism of Avrami-Erofeev equation. In the cases of CuO and Al/CuO, they could promote the O-NO2 bond cleavage and secondary autocatalytic reaction in condensed phase. The effects of these catalysts have some difference in modifying the thermolysis process of NC due to the microstructures of CuO and the addition of Al nanopowders. Furthermore, the presence of Al/CuO(f) can make the Al/CuO(f)-NC composite easier to ignite, whereas the composites have strong resistance to high temperature. Compatibility and thermal safety analysis showed that the Al/CuO had good compatibility with NC and it could be used safely. This contribution suggests that CuO and Al/CuO played key roles in accelerating the thermal decomposition of NC.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper possesses exceptional thermal and electrical conductivity, making it valuable in applications ranging from electronics and heat exchangers to aerospace and energy systems. However, its high reflectivity, thermal conductivity, and susceptibility to oxidation present significant challenges in laser additive manufacturing (AM). This review presents a comprehensive overview of the current state of laser AM of copper and copper alloys, with a focus on laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) techniques. The key processing challenges are outlined, including limited laser absorption with infrared lasers, melt pool instability, and porosity formation. Strategies to enhance the processability of copper and its alloys are critically reviewed, including process parameter optimization, material modifications, and the use of alternative laser sources such as green and blue lasers. The role of process monitoring is also discussed as a pathway to ensure process stability and repeatability. The review further highlights recent applications of copper AM and identifies the transition from density-driven optimization to function-oriented qualification as a key requirement for industrial implementation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is an emerging additive manufacturing technique that is currently adopted by a number of industries for its ability to directly fabricate complex near-net-shaped components with minimal material wastage. Two major limitations of LPBF, however, are that the process inherently produces components containing some amount of porosity and that fabricated components tend to suffer from poor repeatability. While recent advances have allowed the porosity level to be reduced to a minimum, consistent porosity-free fabrication remains elusive. Therefore, it is important to understand how porosity affects mechanical properties in alloys fabricated this way in order to inform the safe design and application of components. To this aim, this article will review recent literature on the effects of porosity on tensile properties, fatigue life, impact and fracture toughness, creep response, and wear behavior. As the number of alloys that can be fabricated by this technology continues to grow, this overview will mainly focus on four alloys that are commonly fabricated by LPBF—Ti-6Al-4 V, Inconel 718, AISI 316L, and AlSi10Mg.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive processes like Laser Beam Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB) result in a distinctive microstructure characterized by metastability, supersaturation, and finesse. Post-process heat treatments modify microstructural features and tune mechanical behavior. However, the exposition at high temperatures can induce changes in the microstructure. Therefore, the present work focuses on the analyses of the tensile response at room and high (200 °C) temperature of the A357 (AlSi7Mg0.6) alloy processed by PBF-LB and subjected to tailored T5 (direct aging) and T6R (rapid solution treatment, quenching, and aging) treatments. Along with the effect of microstructural features in the as-built T5 and T6R alloy, the role of typical process-related defects is also considered. In this view, the structural integrity of the alloy is evaluated by a deep analysis of the work-hardening behavior, and quality indexes have been compared. Results show that T5 increases tensile strength at room temperature without compromising ductility. T6R homogenizes the microstructure and enhances the structural integrity by reducing the detrimental effect of defects, resulting in the best trade-off between strength and ductility. At 200 °C, tensile properties are comparable, but if resilience and toughness moduli are considered, as-built and T5 alloys show the best overall mechanical performance.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The present study demonstrates that the corrosion behavior of dental cobalt–chromium (Co–Cr) alloys is strongly influenced by the interaction between microstructure, manufacturing technique, and oral chemical environment. A comparative investigation was conducted on Co–Cr specimens fabricated using four technological routes: conventional casting, CAD/CAM machining, Selective Laser Melting (SLM), and Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS). The study included microstructural characterization, evaluation of generalized corrosion behavior using the rotating electrode technique, assessment of localized crevice corrosion, and quantitative analysis of the release of twenty metallic cations. Extraction tests were performed for 168 h in two media simulating aggressive oral environments: 0.07 N HCl (acidic medium) and a fluoride-containing electrolyte (0.1% NaF + 0.1% KF). Electrochemical measurements were recorded in the current density range of 10−10 to 10−7 A/cm2, while released cation concentrations were quantified at the µg/L level. All alloys exhibited very low corrosion current densities (icorr in the 10−8 to 10−9 A·cm−2 range), confirming overall good corrosion resistance. Among all manufacturing routes, CAD/CAM specimens demonstrated the highest electrochemical performance, with a wide passivity domain extending up to approximately 740 mV/SCE. A statistical interaction analysis between extraction media and manufacturing techniques was performed using the non-parametric Mann–Whitney (MW) U test. Among the analyzed elements, only chromium showed a statistically significant difference between media (p < 0.05), with an approximately 25-fold-higher release in acidic conditions compared with the fluoride medium, confirming the predominant role of proton-induced destabilization of the protective Cr2O3 passive film. In contrast, fluoride-containing media induced selective release of elements such as Cu (3× higher), W (2.5× higher), and Mo (1.4× higher), associated with complexation phenomena. The manufacturing route significantly influences corrosion behavior. Although additive manufacturing technologies (SLM/DMLS) enable highly accurate and customized prosthetic designs, rapid solidification and microstructural heterogeneities may increase susceptibility to localized corrosion compared with more homogeneous CAD/CAM materials. Clinically, these findings suggest that future restorative strategies should incorporate corrosion-aware material selection within digital workflows. As digital dentistry evolves, predictive models integrating patient-specific oral conditions may assist clinicians in selecting the most appropriate material system for long-term performance. In conclusion, the long-term success of dental Co–Cr prosthetic devices depends not only on mechanical strength and precision of fit, but also on sustained electrochemical stability in the complex oral environment.</jats:p>

Mirror fabrication using metal additive manufacturing in alsi10mg: powder contamination and mitigation methods. Engineering Research Express, 8:075403, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/2631-8695/ae545f, doi:10.1088/2631-8695/ae545f. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides a quantitative AlSi10Mg LPBF contamination case study involving titanium and stainless-steel particles, but it does not report a Ti6Al4V–maraging-steel case. SEM/EDS identified titanium, aluminium, and vanadium as consistent with Ti6Al4V; normalized measurements for Ti, Al, and V averaged approximately 77%, 18%, and 6%, respectively. The authors note that elevated Al may reflect the AlSi10Mg substrate, while the origin of excess V is uncertain. Oxide inclusions were primarily interpreted as Al2O3, with measured compositions near the expected ~53 wt% Al and ~47 wt% O, and averaged values excluding a background-affected measurement of approximately 51% Al and 49% O. A foreign steel inclusion containing Fe, Cr, Ni, and Mo was attributed to 316L, with an estimated composition of ~64% Fe, ~22% Cr, ~14% Ni, ~3% Mo, and ~1% Mn. SEM/EDS observations linked every observed scratch to an inclusion; fragments were inferred to detach and drag across the mirror surface. Oxide inclusions generally produced shorter and thinner scratches than metallic inclusions, although this was not directly quantified. The excerpt mentions Cu as absent in the 316L identification rationale, but specifies no Cu or Sn contamination limits or acceptance thresholds. Gallium from FIB milling and carbon from the SEM environment were recognized as system contaminants.

From text 'gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44'.

The excerpt does not provide exact field evidence that a metal-AM operation uses a powder-specific dedicated sieve station and vacuum to prevent cross-contamination. No observation of such equipment or operating practice appears in the supplied text, so that claim cannot be attributed to this study excerpt. The text instead presents prescriptive guidance and recommendations. ISO/ASTM 52928 recommends closed-loop powder transfer to minimize atmospheric contamination and operator contact, and requires traceability of transfers and processing events, including sieving. It also states that reusable containers, including metal hoppers, should be designated for a single alloy base and thoroughly cleaned between different batches to reduce cross-contamination. A stronger single-alloy recommendation is attributed to NASA: different alloys within a machine are considered an unacceptable cross-contamination risk, and each L-PBF machine supplied by NASA suppliers is required to be dedicated to one alloy. Thus, the excerpt supports powder-specific container use and NASA’s single-alloy printer requirement, but not the claimed dedicated sieve-station-and-vacuum observation. These should be distinguished from the study’s description of standards-based recommendations rather than presented as direct operational field observations.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The significant advancement in additive technologies has made it possible to manufacture metal components in diverse shapes and sizes. Despite this progress, numerous processes and phenomena, along with the implications of producing components layer by layer on their performance under stress, remain inadequately explored. These factors not only affect microstructure but subsequently also the mechanical properties. The positioning of objects within the 3D printer’s workspace can thus significantly play a crucial role in their operational functionality, reliability, and safety of the equipment in an application. This article studies anisotropic properties and the influence of the printing orientation of aluminum alloy (AlSi10Mg) cylindrical tensile samples fabricated through an additive approach on their mechanical properties under tensile loading. Tensile testing of specimens covering seven different spatial orientations in the workspace of a 3D printing machine was performed according to ISO 6892-1 international standard. Minimum and maximum tensile properties (yield and ultimate tensile strength) have been observed in Y-sample and X-sample series, respectively. In contrast, elastic modulus of the 3D printed specimens was minimal for X-sample series, and maximal for Y-sample series. Fracture surfaces of the samples in seven basic spatial orientations were evaluated in synergy with the mechanical testing results determined by optical, electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) textural analysis to find correlation between the strength of the samples and the orientation of grains, their size and morphology. Furthermore, thermodynamic and Scheil–Gulliver simulation has been employed in order to explain the formation of intermetallic phases during additive manufacturing and further justifying observations in microstructure and mechanical properties. The disparity in texture intensity between these regions for samples Y(3) is likely responsible for localized mechanical incompatibilities and strain heterogeneity, resulting in preferential crack paths and reduced mechanical strength compared to the sample Z(3), which presented a more randomized orientation distribution with less distinguishable texture zones, enabling better strain accommodation and more uniform plastic deformation, which correlates with its higher tensile and yield strength.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF)-processed AlSi10Mg produces highly heterogeneous microstructures, where fine α-Al cells, Si-rich networks, and melt-pool boundaries govern local mechanical behavior. Nanoindentation has emerged as a key tool for probing these variations, yet systematic understanding of the links between processing parameters, microstructure, and nano-mechanical response remains limited. This critical review examines how laser processing parameters influence local mechanical response through their impact on microstructural features. Key challenges in interpreting nanoindentation are highlighted, alongside inconsistencies in experimental protocols and reporting practices that hinder cross-study comparisons. Beyond summarizing existing findings, underexplored aspects of nanoindentation in LPBF AlSi10Mg are identified, including spatially correlated microstructure-mechanical mapping, depth-resolved measurements, and integration with advanced characterization and data-driven approaches. By synthesizing current knowledge and clarifying methodological constraints, this review positions nanoindentation not merely as a descriptive tool, but as a mechanistically informed approach for linking processing conditions, microstructural heterogeneity, and local mechanical response. These insights aim to support more rigorous interpretation of small-scale mechanical data and to guide future studies toward predictive understanding and rational process optimization in additively manufactured aluminum alloys.</jats:p>

The excerpt supports treating aluminum powder and water-wet cleaning waste as a potentially hazardous metal–water reaction system rather than assuming water is automatically a safe dust-control method. At elevated temperatures or where fresh metal surfaces are exposed, metal–water reactions can generate explosive hydrogen; removal or damage of the protective oxide film increases the exposed metal/water interface and promotes H2 formation. The review specifically identifies wet dust collection and water-deluge systems as situations requiring particular concern. It also describes an aluminum-dust pretreatment approach using alumina and chromium oxide inhibition films to prevent water from contacting the metallic core, although this is not a substitute for a site-specific laboratory safety assessment. The article references NFPA 484 as the combustible-metals standard, making it a relevant source for aluminum-dust hazard controls. However, this excerpt does not provide detailed procedures for sonication, alkali solutions, solvent flammability or static control, metal-rated vacuum selection, Class D extinguisher use, prohibition of ordinary vacuums or compressed-air jets, or whether wet aluminum waste containers should be sealed or vented. Those questions require consultation of current NFPA 484 requirements, institutional EHS procedures, equipment manufacturer guidance, and a competent safety professional. ## pqac-00000067

From text 'sullivan2010ignitioncombustionand pages 144-149'.

K Sullivan. Ignition, combustion and tuning of nanocomposite thermites. Unknown journal, 2010.

The excerpt documents deliberately prepared aluminum–copper oxide nanothermites, not dilute or accidental bronze contamination. Nano-Al consisted of approximately 70% aluminum and 30% native Al2O3 by mass, with ~50 nm primary particles and a 2–5 nm passivating oxide shell. The synthesized CuO had ~6 nm primary particles; commercial CuO was specified as smaller than 50 nm. Thermite samples were made by weighing stoichiometric amounts of nano-Al and oxidizer, adding hexane, and sonicating for about 30 minutes to promote intimate particle-scale mixing. For rapid-heating tests, mixtures were deposited on a 76 μm platinum wire and heated at approximately 5×10^5 K/s in air. Ignition was operationally defined as the onset of optical emission measured by a photomultiplier. Under these conditions, Al/CuO had a reported ignition temperature of 1217 ± 40 K, compared with a bulk CuO melting/decomposition temperature of 1599 K. The discussion attributes ignition partly to gaseous oxygen released during CuO decomposition to Cu2O, which can generate a critical oxygen partial pressure. The excerpt does not discuss the balanced reaction equation explicitly, micron-scale aluminum dispersed in bronze, AlSi10Mg trace contamination, or spontaneous hazards arising from such contamination; therefore it provides no direct literature evidence for that scenario.


---

## pqac-00000068

From text 'sullivan2010ignitioncombustionand pages 140-144'.

K Sullivan. Ignition, combustion and tuning of nanocomposite thermites. Unknown journal, 2010.

The excerpt documents deliberately prepared nano-Al/CuO thermite experiments under controlled, rapidly heated conditions, rather than spontaneous reaction from dilute contamination. A temperature-jump apparatus heated small samples at approximately 10^6 K/s using a pulsed wire; ignition and combustion were monitored optically or by mass spectrometry. In nano-Al/CuO, ignition delay increased with aluminum oxide-shell thickness, which the cited authors attributed to aluminum diffusion through the Al2O3 shell. The broader discussion reports that rapidly heated nano-Al forms a 2–3 nm oxide shell, may ignite near the aluminum melting point in gaseous oxidizing environments, and that nanoparticle agglomeration and sintering can substantially affect effective particle size and reactivity. Related shock-tube work measured an ignition temperature of about 1400 K for Al/Fe2O3 and 1800 K for Al/MoO3 in inert environments, while composite combustion temperatures were 2750–3350 K; these values are not CuO-specific but illustrate the severe thermal conditions used to study nanothermites. The excerpt does not discuss bronze particles, copper-alloy contamination, AlSi10Mg, trace CuO/Cu contamination, or spontaneous hazards arising from bronze-to-AlSi10Mg contact. It therefore supports a distinction between intentionally mixed, nanoscale, near-stoichiometric thermite formulations subjected to rapid heating and dilute oxidized-metal contamination in an industrial alloy, but provides no literature evidence about the latter hazard.

URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/nano10040725, doi:10.3390/nano10040725. This article has 43 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt documents intentionally prepared Al/CuO nanothermites, not incidental bronze-to-aluminum contamination. CuO morphologies were synthesized hydrothermally: bamboo leaf-like CuO used 120 °C for 8 h, while flaky CuO used 180 °C for 16 h. Aluminum nanopowder was then combined with CuO by ultrasonic dispersion at an Al:CuO molar ratio of 1.33:1, indicating a deliberately formulated near-stoichiometric thermite composition. The article characterized the materials by SEM, TEM, EDS, and XRD, and examined their thermal behavior using DSC under nitrogen from room temperature to 300 °C at multiple heating rates. For compatibility testing with nitrocellulose, Al/CuO and CuO were physically mixed with NC at a 1:19 mass ratio and evaluated at 10 °C/min. It does not report spontaneous ignition, accidental reaction, or a hazard assessment for trace bronze contamination in AlSi10Mg. ## pqac-00000070

From text 'sullivan2010ignitioncombustionand pages 149-153'.

K Sullivan. Ignition, combustion and tuning of nanocomposite thermites. Unknown journal, 2010.

The excerpt documents experimentally induced reaction behavior for a deliberately prepared nano-Al/nano-CuO thermite, rather than spontaneous reaction in dilute or accidentally contaminated bronze. At high heating rates of approximately 10^6 K/s, the system is heated from room temperature to the target temperature in about 1 ms. For nano-Al/6 nm CuO, a pulse to 1473 K followed by a 10 ms hold produced dramatic morphological changes: the fine CuO particles converted into much larger, nearly spherical copper product, while the aluminum particles deformed and the oxide product contacted the copper. The authors interpret the morphology as evidence of substantial reactive sintering, although they could not determine whether sintering preceded reaction or vice versa. Separate CuO experiments showed only mild sintering at 1250 K under a 1 ms hold, indicating strong dependence on temperature and dwell time. Abstract:
Piping system failures in process industries pose significant financial, environmental, and social risks, with inadequate design and corrosion being major contributors. This review synthesizes the academic and normative literature on pipeline design and anticorrosive protection strategies, providing a comprehensive examination of pipeline layout determination, material selection, and methods for mitigating corrosion. A particular focus is placed on organic coating as a pivotal strategy for corrosion reduction, with in-depth insights into their selection and evaluation criteria. By highlighting best practices and advancements in design and protection strategies, this review aims to enhance the overall integrity and safety of piping systems. The findings are intended to support industry professionals in implementing more effective measures to prevent pipeline failures and improve system reliability, while also presenting recent advances and current demands.

Abstract:
To investigate the granule reaction of two-micron aluminum powders with water at low temperatures, differential scanning calorimetry was used to analyze the initial exothermic temperature. Additionally, adiabatic accelerated calorimetry was employed to study the exothermic reaction under adiabatic conditions. The hydrogen production and particle size variation were investigated in order to gain insights into the Al-water reaction in a reactor with no induction time. Through focused beam reflectance measurement analysis, it was observed that during the reaction process of Al-water, particle sizes initially increased and then decreased. Specifically, the particle size of 3 µm aluminum powder experienced a 189% increase after the reaction while 25 µm aluminum powder decreased by 29%. Ultimately, both types of particles reached similar final sizes around 13.89 µm. The process of Al-water reaction was explained and hydrogen production was analyzed, and the kinetic model was obtained.

Abstract:
A new method is proposed to generate hydrogen in situ at low pressure from powder-pressed recycled aluminum turnings activated with small amounts of NaOH and drops of water. The contribution of this system is that the user can obtain small flows of high-purity hydrogen (>99%) to charge their portable electronic devices in remote places, in a simple, controlled, and safe way, since only water is used. Test tubes that contain tiny amounts of NaOH on their surface can be transported and used without contact. In addition to being a safer system, a smaller amount of NaOH and water is needed compared to other systems, there is no need to preheat the water, and the system can even generate heat. As the feeding is drop by drop, the hydrogen flow can be easily controlled by manual or automatic dosing. The waste obtained is solid and contains mostly aluminum hydroxide with some NaOH and impurities from the waste of origin, which are easy to sell and recycle. A study has been carried out to optimize the type of test tubes and establish critical parameters. The results show that a constant and controllable flow rate of hydrogen can be obtained depending on the drip frequency where the chemical reaction predominates over diffusion, that the optimal amount of NaOH is 20 wt%, that a finer grain size can increase the H2 yield with respect to the stoichiometric value but reduces the instantaneous flow with respect to that obtained with larger grains, and that it is very important to control the density and the impurities to increase porosity and therefore water diffusion. The estimated cost of the hydrogen produced is 3.15 EUR/kgH2 and an energy density of 1.12 kWh/kg was achieved with a test tube of 92% aluminum purity and 20 wt% NaOH.

{"answer": "# Cleaning test sieves when changing from bronze to aluminum LPBF powder

**Recommendation.** For LPBF feedstock, obtain a **separate, labeled 63 µm and 250 µm sieve set for aluminum alloys**, together with dedicated collection pans and powder-contact tools. Cleaning the bronze sieves is appropriate for maintaining the sieves, but **visual cleanliness alone does not qualify their next aluminum batch as free of Cu–Sn particles**. If immediate reuse is unavoidable, treat the first aluminum batch as *quarantined* until a documented cleaning, inspection, and powder-comparison check has passed. # Cleaning test sieves when changing from bronze to aluminum LPBF powder

**Recommendation.** For LPBF feedstock, obtain a **separate, labeled 63 µm and 250 µm sieve set for aluminum alloys**, together with dedicated collection pans and powder-contact tools. Cleaning the bronze sieves is appropriate for maintaining the sieves, but **visual cleanliness alone does not qualify their next aluminum batch as free of Cu–Sn particles**. If immediate reuse is unavoidable, treat the first aluminum batch as *quarantined* until a documented cleaning, inspection, and powder-comparison check has passed. This is a conservative laboratory recommendation, **not a claim that ASTM E11 or ISO/ASTM 52907 mandates dedicated sieves**. Particles smaller than either sieve opening can pass with the product, and published AlSi10Mg parts have contained foreign-alloy inclusions after powder changes. (mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42, atkins2026mirrorfabricationusing pages 13-15)

## 1. What the standards and sieve manufacturers establish

**Separate sieve construction, analytical method, and feedstock-quality requirements.** ASTM **E11** and ISO **3310-1** specify woven-wire test sieves and their apertures; ASTM **B214**, ISO **4497**, and **MPIF Standard 05** concern sieve analysis of metal powders. ISO/ASTM **52907** addresses characterization of AM metal powders, including particle-size and chemical-composition methods. None of the available passages from those sources establishes a universal bronze-to-aluminum sieve-decontamination recipe, an ultrasonic frequency, or a permissible number of retained foreign particles. ASTM **E2427**, ISO **2591-1**, ASTM **F3049**, ISO/ASTM **52904**, and NASA **MSFC-SPEC-3717** should not be cited as prescribing a specific cleaning time or proving a shared sieve clean without checking the applicable full editions; the retrieved evidence does not establish such a provision. (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42)

Manufacturer instructions provide the more useful operational distinction:

| Sieve | Dry removal after bronze | If particles remain | Damage to avoid |
|---|---|---|---|
| **250 µm, No. 60** | Invert over a bronze-waste collector; gently tap the **frame** and, if needed, gently brush the **underside only** in a circular motion using a clean, soft nylon brush. | Use a compatible, manufacturer-approved ultrasonic cleaning cycle; rinse and completely dry before reuse. | Hard or wire brushes, pressing powder through openings, needles, forceful air jets, and overloading. |
| **63 µm, No. 230** | Invert and gently tap the frame; collect loose particles without rubbing the cloth. A suitable powder-rated vacuum may remove accessible loose residue **without touching or drawing on the mesh**. | Prefer ultrasonic cleaning **if the sieve construction and laboratory safety assessment permit it**; otherwise retire or reserve it for bronze rather than forcing out lodged particles. | **Avoid brushing this fine mesh**, including vigorous underside brushing; never use a pick, needle, or concentrated air jet. |

Advantech recommends gentle underside-only nylon brushing between tests for **No. 100 and coarser** sieves, but avoiding brushing finer than No. 100; it warns that compressed-air jets locally distort fine openings and that lodged particles should not be picked out. Another section describes particular care beyond No. 80. Thus the 250 µm sieve is brushable with care, whereas the 63 µm sieve is not a good candidate for brushing. Neikov and Yefimov also note that overloading wedges particles into openings and recommend microscopic examination for distorted or torn cloth. A metal-powder vacuum is a **proposed contained-removal option**, not permission from these manufacturers to use an ordinary shop vacuum. (mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 13-14, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18, neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4)

**Wet cleaning parameters are maker-dependent, not ASTM E11 settings.** Retsch guidance says to ultrasonically clean meshes finer than **500 µm** in water with *mild detergent* for approximately **3–5 minutes**, rinse thoroughly, and dry upright; both sieves in this question meet that size criterion. An Advantech *L3P sonic-sifter accessory* manual instead describes a cleaner rated **150 W or less**, mild dishwashing-detergent solution at **24–27 °C**, tap-water rinse, and air drying, and cautions against prolonged sonication. Its component-specific restrictions must not be assumed to apply to every round sieve. Neither cited instruction supplies a bath frequency: **40 kHz is not a verified requirement here**. If the sieve manufacturer approves your specific round sieves for aqueous ultrasonics, a short, monitored **3–5-minute room-temperature** cycle is a defensible *Retsch-derived starting point*, not a cross-alloy cleanliness validation. Thoroughly remove detergent, rinse with suitable clean water where permitted, and dry fully; avoid leaving water or cleaning residues that could contaminate aluminum feedstock. (bath2003finetuningsieve pages 3-4, separatorUnknownyearmodell3p pages 10-15, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18)

**Check the actual mesh-to-frame bond before choosing heat or liquid.** An Advantech account of *soldered* sieves says to keep the sieve below **149 °C** in its described wet-sieving procedure; that number is **not an approved drying temperature for an epoxy-bonded sieve**. The L3P manual prohibits heating its own stack components. For an unidentified round sieve, use ambient, upright drying or a maker-approved low-temperature method; get the sieve maker’s limits for its epoxy, solder, sealant, and frame before oven drying or solvent immersion. Replace torn, slack, or distorted cloth rather than repairing a precision 63 µm sieve with solder or epoxy: localized solder heat distorts openings, and epoxy blocks openings or can fracture. Avoid solvent ultrasonics unless the bath and solvent procedure are specifically approved for flammable-liquid service. (mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 13-14, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18, separatorUnknownyearmodell3p pages 10-15, bath2003finetuningsieve pages 3-4)

## 2. Why LPBF calls for stricter changeover control

ISO/ASTM **52907** provides methods for characterizing powder, **not proof that an apparently clean sieve yields chemically uncontaminated powder**. Powder-life-cycle guidance summarized in the retrieved literature calls for tracking operations including sieving, assigning reusable hoppers to an alloy base, and cleaning between batches. A secondary source reports a stricter NASA **single-alloy-per-LPBF-machine** policy; that is a machine requirement as reported there, **not a verified NASA requirement to dedicate every handheld sieve**. In an observed AM facility, NIOSH documented feedstock-specific external vacuums and identified migrated powder particles on facility surfaces using SEM–EDX. These observations support dedicated powder-contact equipment as prudent practice, while showing that nearby tools, gloves, and surfaces also matter. (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 16-23, stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 23-29)

The evidence for consequences is material, but **not a measured Cu–Sn-in-AlSi10Mg dose–response**:

* In a controlled Ti-6Al-4V/maraging-steel powder study, SEM–BSE plus particle-resolved EDS identified deliberately added **0.5, 1, and 2.5 wt%** foreign powder. At **0.5 wt% maraging steel in Ti64**, bulk-area EDS reported Fe as **not detectable**, although individual foreign particles were identified; ordinary bulk-property or bulk-composition screening can therefore miss discrete particles. The authors also documented foreign-alloy inclusions at fracture regions in related PBF examples, including an inclusion associated with crack initiation. **0.5 wt% was a tested detection case, not an acceptable contamination limit.** DOI: **10.3390/ma12152342**. (santecchia2019crosscontaminationquantificationin pages 1-3, santecchia2019crosscontaminationquantificationin pages 3-6, santecchia2019crosscontaminationquantificationin pages 6-9)
* An AlSi10Mg LPBF mirror study identified Ti-6Al-4V and probable 316L inclusions by SEM–EDS and associated observed scratches with inclusions. It implicated both printer powder interchange and contamination from the broader production environment; even a printer assigned only AlSi10Mg showed evidence consistent with environmental transfer. It also noted that a nominal **60 µm** sieve cannot remove smaller inclusions—many observed oxides were **<50 µm**. This demonstrates the limitation of trying to *sieve away* chemically different particles in the LPBF size range; it does **not** establish a Cu–Sn-specific cracking or corrosion threshold. DOI: **10.1088/2631-8695/ae545f**. (atkins2026mirrorfabricationusing pages 6-9, atkins2026mirrorfabricationusing pages 13-15, atkins2026mirrorfabricationusing pages 15-17)

An illustrative published AlSi10Mg composition table gives **Cu ≤0.10 wt%** and **Sn ≤0.05 wt%** (approximately **1,000 and 500 ppm by mass**). Its reference list attributes the composition to **ASTM F3318-18**, but the cited full standard and its applicability to your *new* Al alloy were not independently checked. **Composition maxima are not permission to introduce bronze particles:** a batch can meet a bulk Cu number yet contain an isolated Cu–Sn inclusion. Set acceptance against the actual feedstock specification and uncontaminated baseline. For example, if baseline Cu is 700 ppm and a 1,000-ppm maximum applies, the *arithmetic* bulk allowance is 300 ppm—**not** a demonstrated permissible foreign-particle level. (karolewska2025improvingthemechanical pages 5-7, karolewska2024improvingthemechanical media 2e0cbe01, karolewska2025improvingthemechanical pages 23-24, santecchia2019crosscontaminationquantificationin pages 1-3)

## 3. Cleaning verification and a small-lab changeover SOP

**Evidence grades:** *Manufacturer/handbook supported* below means a documented technique for maintaining sieve integrity; *proposed laboratory control* means an appropriately cautious qualification step **without a universal standard acceptance limit**. Do not turn a negative spot check into a claim of zero contamination.

1. **Before touching the bronze powder, control dust and keep alloys separate.** Identify the sieve construction and condition; label the bronze and aluminum streams, separate their pans, lids, funnels, scoops, wipes, brushes, gloves, and containers. Record sieve IDs, prior alloy, batch, and operator. Work using the lab’s combustible-metal-powder controls, containment, and appropriate PPE; do not shake or bang dusty sieves in the open. *Manufacturer-supported handling plus proposed changeover control.* (mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18, stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 9-13, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44)
2. **Recover bronze without embedding it further.** Empty the **250 µm** sieve and then the **63 µm** sieve over separate designated bronze collectors; gently tap the frames. Gently brush only the underside of the 250 µm cloth with a clean soft nylon brush, if needed. Do **not** brush the 63 µm cloth or force lodged grains through either opening. Clean the frames, rim seams, lid, pan, and contact tools, not merely the visible center of the mesh. Use a vacuum **only if rated and approved for this combustible metal powder**, with an alloy-specific attachment; do not use a shop vacuum or jet powder into the room. *Manufacturer-supported mesh protection; proposed equipment qualification.* (mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 13-14, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18, stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 16-23, reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 2-3)
3. **Inspect before considering wet cleaning.** Examine both faces against a backlight and, preferably, under a stereo microscope; inspect particularly the 63 µm weave, mesh/frame junction, holes, sagging, clogged apertures, and retained bronze-colored grains. Regular microscopic examination and replacement of visibly damaged sieves are supported. A photograph and a **noncontact** tare-mass comparison can document gross residue but **cannot exclude a few particles**. If visible bronze remains in inaccessible joints, reserve or replace the sieve. *Handbook/maker-supported inspection; proposed cleanliness-release decision.* (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4, bath2003finetuningsieve pages 3-4, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18)
4. **Clean further only by an approved route.** For the current **bronze-only residue**, an aqueous mild-detergent ultrasonic cycle, thorough rinsing, and complete upright drying is a manufacturer-derived option **after** checking mesh bonding, bath compatibility, and EHS approval. Follow the *actual sieve maker* where its instructions differ. Do **not** use 149 °C as a default dryer setting or invent a mandatory frequency. Repeat microscopic inspection when dry. If ultrasonics cannot be conducted safely or damage-free, the low-risk answer is **new aluminum sieves**, not increasingly aggressive brushing. *Manufacturer supported, conditional on construction and EHS.* (bath2003finetuningsieve pages 3-4, separatorUnknownyearmodell3p pages 10-15, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18)

NIOSH used tape-mounted SEM–EDX to identify feedstock-like particles and surface wipes to quantify metals; a wiped **mesh face** itself could be damaged, so sample frames and other robust surfaces instead. A clean backlit mesh, no recovered Cu–Sn particles in the *inspected* areas, and no unexplained mass gain are useful screens, **not validated detection limits**. *Analytical methods supported; application and acceptance criteria proposed.* (stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 23-29, stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 16-23, mfg2001testsievingprinciples pages 14-18)

Then take representative samples of the *first retained production fraction* and an unused, same-lot reference. A sacrificial flush is a **proposed process-development measure, not a standard-prescribed amount or substitute for release testing**. (santecchia2019crosscontaminationquantificationin pages 3-6, santecchia2019crosscontaminationquantificationin pages 6-9, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42, stefaniak2025healthhazardevaluation pages 23-29)
